claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops radiation-induced precipitates under energetic-particle irradiation.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits slight irradiation hardening.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 1 vol% Y2O3 nanoparticles during bulk consolidation.
Consolidation will produce evenly distributed Y2O3 dispersoids at grain boundaries and within grains.
Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as stable sinks for irradiation-induced point defects.
The Y2O3 defect sinks will capture irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Point-defect capture by Y2O3 will limit solute diffusion that would otherwise lead to precipitation.
Y2O3 dispersoids will stabilize grain boundaries.
Y2O3 dispersoids will reduce irradiation-associated segregation.
Adding Y2O3 will significantly reduce the formation or growth of radiation-induced precipitates relative to the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening after exposure to approximately 8 dpa.
Adding approximately 1 vol% Y2O3 will improve the alloy's suitability for large-scale bulk fabrication.
Spark plasma sintering or a similar route is suitable for industrial bulk fabrication of the proposed composite.
The proposed behavior applies up to approximately 8 dpa at temperatures typical of fusion first-wall components.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes irradiation hardening as negligible or as being retained at a negligible level, whereas the initial-state and baseline fields describe a slight measurable increase in hardness. These terms may overlap experimentally, but no quantitative definition reconciles them.
